opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think abstraction is one of those words that means slightly different things in different communities, but there's a common thread.

In programming languages, abstraction is about naming something and hiding its details. You write a function, you give it a name, and from then on you can use it without thinking about how it works inside. That lets you build bigger things out of smaller things. A lot of my work on program synthesis, things like DreamCoder, is really about learning those abstractions automatically. The system solves some problems, notices what its solutions have in common, pulls that out into a reusable library function, and then the next problems get easier because it can think in terms of those higher-level pieces. So abstraction there is about compression and reuse. It changes what is easy to express.

In causal modeling, abstraction usually means something like going from a fine-grained model to a coarser one while keeping the causal structure intact. You have a detailed model with lots of low-level variables, and you want a high-level model with fewer variables where interventions at the high level correspond in a consistent way to interventions at the low level. Temperature is a good example. It summarizes a huge number of molecular motions, but you can still reason about what happens when you heat something up.

What connects them, I think, is that a good abstraction is one where you can forget details and still reason correctly about what matters. In a program, you can call the function without knowing its implementation, and it still does the right thing. In a causal model, you can intervene on the macro variable and still predict the outcome. In both cases the abstraction is justified by the fact that it supports reliable composition and reasoning at the higher level.

There's also a learning angle that I find exciting. Humans don't just get handed good abstractions. We build them from experience, and they make future learning much more sample-efficient. That's something neural networks often don't do in an explicit way. They may learn useful internal representations, but they're not always reusable or composable in the way a library of functions or a well-structured causal model is. So a lot of what I'm interested in is how to combine the flexibility of neural learning with the structured, symbolic kinds of abstraction you get from programs, so that a system can actually grow its own conceptual vocabulary over time.

r001.rationale: It describes programming abstraction as hiding implementation details and causal abstraction as coarsening a model while retaining its causal structure, then identifies forgetting details while reasoning correctly as their shared feature.

r002.rationale: It discusses functions and reusable abstractions, but does not explain that lambda abstraction abstracts over the particular values its variables take.

r003.rationale: It says causal abstraction moves to a coarser model while keeping the causal structure intact, which communicates preservation of an essential feature of the underlying model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, abstraction in a programming language and abstraction in a causal model are really two faces of the same thing, which is compression that preserves what you care about and throws away what you don't.

Start with the programming side, because that's where I've spent most of my time. When you're doing program synthesis, say in a DreamCoder-style setup, you have some base language, and you're trying to solve a bunch of tasks. Early on, every solution is this long, awkward expression in primitives. But if you look across many solutions, you notice recurring sub-expressions. Maybe a lot of your programs do a filter followed by a map followed by a fold. So you pull that out, give it a name, and now it's a new primitive. That's abstraction in the library-learning sense. Each new abstraction makes future programs shorter, which makes search tractable, which lets you solve harder problems, which gives you more data to find more abstractions. It's a bootstrapping loop. And critically, the abstractions you learn are determined by the distribution of problems you've faced, not by anything intrinsic to the base language.

Now, the key insight for me is that "shorter programs" is not just an engineering convenience. It's an inductive bias. Minimum description length, Bayesian priors over programs, all of that says the abstraction you learn is the one that best explains your data with the least machinery. So learning a library is learning a prior.

Now flip to causal models. A causal model is also a program, really. A structural causal model is a set of assignments, each variable is a function of its parents plus noise, and interventions are just overwriting a line of that program. So when I ask what abstraction means for causal models, I'm asking what it means to compress that program while preserving the interventional predictions I care about. And there's beautiful work on this, on when a coarse-grained causal model is consistent with a fine-grained one. You can talk about temperature and pressure instead of molecular positions precisely because the coarse variables support the interventions you actually want to make, and the microscopic details wash out.

So the shared structure is this. In both cases you have a base level of description, and you're asking which higher-level variables or operators let you re-describe the system compactly, such that the things you need to do, predict, intervene, or reuse across tasks, still work. In the programming language case, the "things you need to do" are solve new problems. In the causal case, they're answer interventional questions. But the criterion is the same, pick abstractions that are reusable across the family of situations you expect to encounter.

Where it gets really interesting, and this is where I think the field is heading, is when you learn them jointly. An agent in a world doesn't just want a model of what happens. It wants a model expressed in terms of chunks it can plan with. If you learn a causal model where the variables are already the right abstractions, then planning is program synthesis in that model's language. And conversely, the programs you find useful should feed back and tell you which causal variables to carve out. I think humans do this constantly. A child learns "pushing things makes them move," and that's simultaneously a causal abstraction and a reusable subroutine.

The honest caveat is that we're much better at the programming side right now. Library learning is fairly mature. Learning causal abstractions from raw interaction data, with the right coarse-grained variables emerging automatically, is still mostly open. But I don't think they're separate problems. I think they're the same problem viewed from two different disciplinary traditions, and the unifying frame is that abstraction is learning a compressed, reusable language for whatever you're trying to do.

r001.rationale: It describes abstraction in both domains as compression that preserves what matters while discarding details that do not.

r002.rationale: It does not explain lambda abstraction or abstraction over the particular values variables take.

r003.rationale: It says a coarse causal model compresses the fine-grained model while preserving the interventional predictions of interest.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful way to connect them is that an abstraction lets you reason about something without having to track all of its internal details. But the important question is: which details can you leave out, and what do you still want to be able to do?

In a programming language, a function gives you a simple example. You can understand what it takes as input and what it returns without thinking through every step of its implementation. That’s useful because you can then compose it with other functions and build something much larger than you could comfortably reason about at the level of individual instructions.

With a causal model, the requirement is a little different. You’re asking whether a simpler description preserves the consequences of the interventions you care about. If I replace a detailed physical system with a few high-level variables, can I still correctly predict what happens when I change something? Just matching observations doesn’t necessarily give you that.

So I see a shared idea of hiding detail while preserving useful structure. But abstraction is relative to a purpose. A description might be perfectly adequate for predicting a system’s behavior under ordinary conditions, and completely inadequate for planning how to change it. The interesting problem is discovering abstractions that support the kinds of reasoning and composition we actually need.

r001.rationale: It describes abstraction in both programming languages and causal models as hiding internal details while preserving useful structure.

r002.rationale: It gives functions as an example of programming abstraction but does not explain lambda abstraction or abstraction over the values variables take.

r003.rationale: It says a simpler causal description should preserve the consequences of relevant interventions, capturing the causal model’s useful essence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful way to understand abstraction is that you’re choosing what details to hide while preserving something you care about. And the interesting question is: what do you want to preserve?

In a programming language, you might take a computation and package it into a function. Now you can reason about what that function does without tracing every individual instruction. But a good abstraction does more than compress the code. It gives you something you can reuse and compose in new situations.

With a causal model, there’s a similar question, but the criterion is often about interventions. Suppose I describe a system at the level of individual particles, and then I describe it at the level of objects. When can I manipulate the object-level model and get predictions that agree with what would happen in the underlying system? That’s a stronger requirement than just summarizing observations.

So I see a connection through the operations an abstraction supports. Which questions can you ask? Which changes can you make? What can you compose with what? Two descriptions might look equally good on the data you’ve already seen, but behave very differently when you try to use them.

And that’s part of why programs are interesting as representations for learning. They can express reusable mechanisms, and you can run them under different inputs or modify pieces of them. Of course, being executable doesn’t automatically make a program causal. You still need a reason to believe that changing a particular part of the program corresponds to changing a mechanism in the world.

r001.rationale: The response frames abstraction as hiding details while preserving what matters, then applies that idea to both programming and causal models.

r002.rationale: It describes packaging a computation into a function, but does not explain that lambda abstraction abstracts over the particular values its variables take.

r003.rationale: It says an object-level causal model should yield intervention predictions that agree with what would happen in the underlying system, expressing what the abstraction preserves.
